segments.arabic:
١٢٠٤٠- أم سارة «١»:
كنود، التي أعطاها حاطب بن أبي بلتعة الكتاب إلى قريش فنزلت فيه: لا تَتَّخِذُوا عَدُوِّي وَعَدُوَّكُمْ أَوْلِياءَ [سورة الممتحنة: آية ١] . سمّاها قتادة عن أنس في حديث مختصر أخرجه ابن مندة، من طريق [....] عن قتادة، عن أنس- أن أمّ سارة أمة لقريش أتت النبيّ ﵌ فشكت إليه الحاجة، ثم إن رجلا بعث معها كتابا إلى أهل مكّة ليحفظوا عياله، فنزلت: يا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لا تَتَّخِذُوا عَدُوِّي وَعَدُوَّكُمْ أَوْلِياءَ ... [سورة الممتحنة آية ١] الآية.
قال أبو نعيم: لا أعلم أحدا ذكرها في الصّحابة ونسبها إلى الإسلام.
قلت: قد ذكروا أنّ النبيّ ﵌ كان أهدر دمها ثم أمّها يوم الفتح.
وقد تقدّم بيان ذلك في سارة. فإنه اختلف في اسمها وكنيتها، فقيل سارة أم كنود، وقيل كنود أم سارة.
segments.english:
12040—Umm Sara:

Kanud, to whom Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a gave the letter for Quraysh; concerning this the following was revealed: “Do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies” [Surat al-Mumtahana, verse 1]. Qatada named her in a brief hadith from Anas, transmitted by Ibn Manda by way of [lacuna], from Qatada, from Anas: Umm Sara, a bondwoman of Quraysh, came to the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and complained to him of her need. Then a man sent with her a letter to the people of Mecca so that they might safeguard his dependents. Thereupon the following was revealed: “O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies ...” [Surat al-Mumtahana, verse 1], to the end of the verse.

Abu Nu'aym said: “I do not know of anyone who included her among the Companions or attributed her to Islam.”

I say: They have mentioned that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had declared her blood forfeit and then [apparently granted her safe-conduct; the Arabic wording is uncertain] on the Day of the Conquest.

An explanation of this has already been given under Sara. Her name and kunya were disputed: she was said to be Sara, Umm Kanud, and she was said to be Kanud, Umm Sara.

unresolved.explanation: The supplied Arabic does not yield the safe-conduct sense naturally. The Urdu witness supports an intended reading equivalent to أمنها, but no Arabic al-Isabah manuscript confirms that restoration.
No supplied witness identifies the missing transmitter or transmitters before Qatada; the lacuna has therefore been preserved.
